The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Feivush, Author of "Beit Shmuel"
The Historical Period and the Background to the Glory of His Work
In the second half of the seventeenth century the world of Torah in Europe went through deep upheavals that changed the face of Torah scholarship and halakhic ruling for generations [cite: 1, 2]. The period after the decrees of Tach and Tat (1648–1649) was marked by a broad migration of Torah scholars from the centers of Torah in Poland westward, toward the German-speaking communities of Ashkenaz [cite: 1, 2]. This migration produced a fruitful encounter between the Polish method of study, whose distinctive mark was sharp pilpul and deep analysis of Talmudic topics, and the Ashkenazi tradition, which strove for order, for defined custom and for practical decision [cite: 1, 2].
At that time, the literature of commentaries on Rabbi Yosef Karo's "Shulchan Arukh" and the glosses of the Rema was in the midst of a flowering [cite: 1, 3]. While comprehensive and systematic commentaries had already been written in the first half of the century on the sections "Orach Chayim" and "Yoreh De'ah," the section "Even HaEzer" – which deals with the laws of marriage, betrothal, divorce and deserted wives – remained relatively neglected in Torah literature [cite: 1]. The severe legal complexity of these laws, together with the heavy halakhic responsibility involved in permitting a married woman to remarry, kept many halakhic authorities away from systematic writing of a comprehensive work on the order of the Shulchan Arukh in this section [cite: 1]. Against this background arose the figure of Rabbi Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Feivush, who produced a thorough and systematic commentary that became one of the most central and indispensable commentaries on the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 1, 2, 4].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life, His Teachers and the Course of His Rabbinic Leadership
Rabbi Shmuel, son of Rabbi Uri Shraga Feivush, was born in the middle of the seventeenth century in the town of Wodzisław (Vaydislav) in Poland [cite: 1, 2, 5]. In his youth he was sent to study in the cradle of Polish Jewish scholarship – the yeshiva of Krakow (Cracow), where he acquired most of his learning from two of the great men of the generation [cite: 1, 2]. His first teacher was Rabbi Yehoshua Heschel ben Rabbi Yaakov, known as "Rabbi R. Heshel," one of the prominent spiritual leaders of the generation [cite: 1, 2]. After the death of Rabbi R. Heshel, Rabbi Shmuel continued his course of study under his successor in the rabbinate and in the headship of the yeshiva of Krakow, Rabbi Aryeh Leib ben Rabbi Zechariah Mendel, known as Rabbi Aryeh Leib "the Tall" [cite: 1, 2, 5].
Rabbi Aryeh Leib recognized his student's superior abilities and took him as son-in-law to his daughter [cite: 1, 2]. This marriage brought Rabbi Shmuel into one of the most distinguished and influential families in the rabbinic world of his day, since his brothers-in-law were renowned Torah scholars, among them Rabbi Yechezkel Yehoshua Feivel Teomim, author of the book "Panim Meirot," and Rabbi Shaul ben Rabbi Heshel of Krakow [cite: 1, 2]. After his marriage Rabbi Shmuel began to hold Torah positions; some sources note that he served as a preacher and "maggid meisharim" in Lvov, although some doubt this fact [cite: 2]. He later was appointed av beit din and mara d'atra in the community of Sydłów in Poland, where he served in the rabbinate and where he began writing his great work [cite: 2, 4].
In the year 5451 (1691) an approach reached him from the council of the community of Fürth in Germany – one of the important and central communities of Ashkenaz – to take upon himself the spiritual leadership of the city [cite: 2]. Rabbi Shmuel accepted the offer and arrived in Fürth in the winter of 5452 (1692), where he served as av beit din, mara d'atra and head of the local yeshiva for about three years [cite: 2]. In the year 5454 (1694) Rabbi Shmuel left Fürth and returned to Poland, to his previous position in Sydłów [cite: 2]. Researchers and early sources raise various conjectures about his sudden departure from Ashkenaz, attributing it to his longing for his native land and for the Polish method of study, or alternatively to internal disputes that had arisen at that time in the community of Fürth [cite: 2]. Rabbi Shmuel led the community of Sydłów until the day of his death and was buried in the city's cemetery [cite: 2]. The date of his death is not definite in the sources, but it is agreed that he died in the first years of the eighteenth century, apparently between 5459 (1699) and 5467 (1706) [cite: 1, 2].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Book "Beit Shmuel": The Scope of the Work, Its Process of Formation and the Printing of "Appei Revrevei"
When he came to compose his book on the section Even HaEzer, Rabbi Shmuel referred explicitly to the state of neglect of the study of this section of the Shulchan Arukh, and recommended on his research the verse "The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone" [cite: 1]. With a linguistic allusion to the word "Even" (stone) – the first letters of "Even HaEzer" – Rabbi Shmuel sought to turn the halakhic section that had repelled many students into the focus of theoretical study and halakhic ruling [cite: 1]. The work was built with great precision, presenting the sources of the law, clarifying the views of the Rishonim and Acharonim, and giving a clear and reasoned decision on the intricate topics of the laws of marriage and divorce [cite: 1, 5, 6].
The book "Beit Shmuel" went through a process of development and halakhic refinement and was published in two main editions during the author's lifetime [cite: 4, 7]. The first edition (the first printing) was printed in 5449 (1689) in the city of Dyhernfurth, in the press of Shabtai Meshorer Bass [cite: 4, 5]. This edition included the running commentary along with fundamental appendices: "Kuntres Agunot," which concisely collects the responses of the halakhic authorities on siman 17, the "Seder HaGet" of Rabbi Yaakov Margalit, and the "Seder Gittin" of Rabbi Yechiel Michel of Krakow with detailed additions and glosses from the study hall of Rabbi Shmuel [cite: 5]. After his move to Fürth, the author devoted himself to a renewed and expanded revision of his work [cite: 2, 4]. The second edition (the later printing) was printed in Fürth in 5454 (1694), in which he corrected objections, added many sources and deepened his analyses [cite: 2, 4]. Our master Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai (the Chida) established in his book "Shem HaGedolim" a decisive bibliographical-halakhic rule, according to which one should pay no heed to the first edition of the book "Beit Shmuel" where it differs from the later edition, since the author himself retracted and corrected his conclusions [cite: 7].
Parameter of Comparison | First Edition (Dyhernfurth, 5449) | Later Edition (Fürth, 5454)
Year and Place of Printing | 1689 (5449), Dyhernfurth [cite: 4, 5] | 1694 (5454), Fürth [cite: 2, 4]
Printing House | The press of Shabtai Meshorer Bass of Prague [cite: 5] | The Fürth press [cite: 2, 4]
Contents of the Appendices | Kuntres Agunot, Seder HaGet and Seder Gittin [cite: 5] | A revised, corrected and expanded text within the body of the commentary [cite: 4, 7]

In parallel with Rabbi Shmuel's work, another great halakhic authority in Poland – Rabbi Moshe Lima, av beit din of Vilna – composed a thorough commentary on the section Even HaEzer called "Chelkat Mechokek" [cite: 1, 3, 5]. The printers of the Shulchan Arukh recognized the superiority of the two works and decided to set them side by side, on both sides of the text of the Shulchan Arukh and the Rema [cite: 1, 3, 4]. The combined edition that included "Chelkat Mechokek" and "Beit Shmuel" received the collective name "Appei Revrevei," based on the Aramaic translation of the expression "great faces," and from then until today the two works are printed together in most editions of the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 1, 2, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Halakhic Method, His Way of Analysis and His Examination of Topics
Rabbi Shmuel's halakhic method in the commentary "Beit Shmuel" distinctly combines deep Polish yeshiva analysis with the demand for clear, practical ruling [cite: 1, 2]. His way of study is characterized by thorough analysis of the legal and halakhic concepts underlying the topics [cite: 6, 8]. Thus, for example, in his discussions concerning a man who betroths a woman against her will, Rabbi Shmuel examines the halakhic mechanism of "talya vezavin" (a purchase made under compulsion) and explains why in forced betrothal of a woman the betrothal does not take effect [cite: 6]. He clarifies that although by biological and legal law the betrothal should have taken effect, the Sages removed it from him ("afkinhu Rabbanan lekiddushin minei") because he acted improperly [cite: 6]. Following this, he compares compulsion of the woman with compulsion of the man: whereas a man who compels a woman does not betroth her because of the Sages' enactment, a man who was compelled to betroth – his betrothal is valid, since it is in his power to divorce her against her will [cite: 6]. This analysis leads him to examine the halakhic implications in our time after the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom forbidding divorcing a woman against her will, examining whether the status of a man who was compelled to betroth has changed, or whether compulsion in betrothal was exempted from this enactment [cite: 6].
Another distinctive feature of Rabbi Shmuel's way is the constant confrontation and meticulous clarification between the differing views of the early halakhic authorities – such as the Rambam, the Raavad, the Ramban, the Rashba, the Rif and the Ran – and the rulings of the Acharonim who preceded him, among them the Taz, the Shach, the Sema and the "Chelkat Mechokek" [cite: 5, 6, 8]. In the laws of a single witness in betrothal and situations of contradiction between witnesses, Rabbi Shmuel analyzes the weight of the "presumption of being unmarried" and its definitions in situations of "two against two" or of a single witness contradicting a woman [cite: 8]. He presents the dispute between the Rambam and the other Rishonim in the case where one witness says "she was betrothed" and another contradicts him, and he is precise in the language of the Shulchan Arukh and the Rema in order to resolve complex contradictions between different simanim in the book [cite: 6, 8].
Beyond the theoretical depth, the style of the "Beit Shmuel" is distinguished by brevity and a rare capacity for concision [cite: 1, 6]. In a few lines Rabbi Shmuel manages to summarize difficult Talmudic topics, to lay out the views of the Rishonim, and to decide the halakha in practice clearly and sharply [cite: 1, 6]. This concentrated style made the work a central working tool for judges and teachers of halakha who need well-grounded decisions in the topics of Even HaEzer [cite: 1, 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Additional Works, His Family, His Students and His Legacy for Generations
Although Rabbi Shmuel's name is forever linked with his commentary on Even HaEzer, the scope of his Torah work went beyond the bounds of this work [cite: 2]. Historical sources and family testimonies teach that Rabbi Shmuel also composed a comprehensive commentary on the section "Yoreh De'ah" of the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 2]. His son-in-law, Rabbi Uri Feivush Hamburger, describes in his introduction to the book "Urim VeTumim" the greatness of his father-in-law and expresses a prayer that he will merit to publish his writings on Yoreh De'ah [cite: 2]. Sadly, these writings did not merit to see print and have not reached us [cite: 2]. Likewise, from his service as head of a yeshiva and av beit din in Sydłów and in Fürth, Rabbi Shmuel composed halakhic responsa and homilies, some of which were absorbed into the books of the sages of his generation [cite: 2, 5].
Rabbi Shmuel raised a splendid dynasty of Torah scholars and rabbinic leaders who influenced European Jewry [cite: 2]. His son, Rabbi Yosef, was the father of Rabbi Shmuel who served as av beit din of Amdur and Minsk (Minsk), and his other sons were Rabbi Aryeh Leib and Rabbi Shilem [cite: 2]. Among his sons-in-law were prominent Rabbi Uri Feivush Hamburger, who later emigrated to London and served as the first chief rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Britain, Rabbi Betzalel Slutsky, and Rabbi Yitzchak Eisik of Amdur [cite: 2]. Rabbi Shmuel's family ties connected him to the most distinguished rabbinic dynasties in Eastern Europe, including the Teomim and Ornstein families and the descendants of Rabbi Shaul Wahl [cite: 2].
During his tenure as head of a yeshiva in Fürth and in Sydłów, Rabbi Shmuel raised many students who served in the rabbinate throughout Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 2]. The Fürth yeshiva under his leadership was considered one of the most attractive Torah centers in Germany [cite: 2]. However, Rabbi Shmuel's main and enduring influence lies in his written legacy [cite: 1, 2, 3]. From the day the second edition of "Beit Shmuel" was printed as part of "Appei Revrevei," the book became a cornerstone of halakhic ruling in the section Even HaEzer [cite: 1, 3, 4]. The greatest halakhic authorities of the following centuries – among them Rabbi Yechezkel Landau, author of the "Noda BiYehuda," Rabbi Moshe Sofer, author of the "Chatam Sofer," the authors of the "Pitchei Teshuva" and the "Arukh HaShulchan," and down to the judges of the rabbinic courts in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries – regard the commentary "Beit Shmuel" as a primary source and a binding starting point in every halakhic discussion of the laws of marriage, divorce and deserted wives [cite: 1, 2, 3].
